                                            PUC PROJECT NO. 58000

     RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                               §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
     WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                           §
     TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                      §                    OF TEXAS
     THE ERCOT REGION                                   §

    LOWER COLORADO RIVER AUTHORITY AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES
      CORPORATION’S COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF
                AMENDMENTS TO §§ 25.192, 25.193, AND 25.252

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

            Lower Colorado River Authority and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation

(collectively LCRA) submit these comments and executive summary in response to Commission

Staff’s proposal for publication (PFP) covering amendments to 16 Texas Administrative Code

(TAC) § 25.192, relating to Transmission Rates for Export from ERCOT, § 25.193, relating to

Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factors (TCRF), and new § 25.252,

relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs.


                                            I.    INTRODUCTION

            Section 6 of Senate Bill (SB) 6 defines two clear principles for the Commission to consider

when evaluating a proper transmission cost recovery mechanism. First, all loads must

appropriately contribute towards the recovery of Transmission Service Providers’ (TSPs) costs to

provide and maintain safe and reliable access to the transmission system.1 Second, the share of

that cost for each customer class should be determined on a cost-causation basis.2 In prior

comments in this project, LCRA has highlighted the diminished ability of the four coincident peak

(4CP) mechanism to preserve these principles. In parallel with this rulemaking effort, state

leadership has been encouraged by the economic growth that large loads bring to Texas but has


1

2
    Id. § 6(b).

LCRA COMMENTS                                                                             Page 1 of 23
 directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas to take action to ensure that costs of

interconnecting these large loads do not burden residential ratepayers.3 LCRA supports the PFP

because it adheres to the direction from state leadership. Specifically, the PFP will result in better

protections for residential ratepayers by adjusting to a twelve coincident peak (12CP) mechanism

and instituting a minimum billing demand charge for large loads. These changes, along with

additional SB 6 implementation issues being addressed in Project No. 58481, Large Load

Interconnection Standards, should work in concert to ensure that large loads are (1) funding an

appropriate amount of transmission costs that are initiated by their interconnection and (2)

becoming long-term partners in the recovery of future transmission costs.

        Although supportive of the approach taken in the PFP, LCRA offers comments and

suggested revisions to the PFP. Presently, it is unclear when the new methodologies will be

effective in terms of billing year and period. LCRA welcomes additional clarity from Commission

Staff, either in the form of a workshop or supplemental documentation filed in this project. In

addition, the duration of the coincident peak should be lengthened from 30 minutes to one hour to

mitigate impacts on wholesale energy prices and reduce implementation costs and complexity.

Finally, the minimum billing demand methodology should be modified to strike a more reasonable

balance between the costs that large loads will bear directly, including their required financial

security, and the costs that benefit – and should therefore be borne by – all users of the transmission

system.

                               II.    RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS

       Question 1:
       Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
       different for large load customers with different contracted peak demand or different non-
       coincident (NCP) demands?
       Response:
       When considering the intent behind this rulemaking (SB 6), the focus of the statute was to

establish an appropriate megawatt (MW) threshold to designate what should be considered a large

load (i.e., 75 MW), and to direct the Commission to establish standards to reliably integrate those

large loads into the ERCOT system. As part of that charge, the Commission is now determining

through this rulemaking the proper methods to ensure that all loads appropriately contribute to the

recovery of transmission costs. LCRA agrees that the proposed minimum billing demand charge

will serve to ensure that large loads appropriately contribute to transmission cost recovery in a fair

and predictable manner over the long term. In finalizing this concept, it is important for the

Commission to recognize that the Legislature did not speak to specific behaviors, business models,

or magnitude tiers of large loads. As such, there should be no differentiation in the application of

the minimum billing demand provision for loads greater than or equal to 75 MW.


       Question 2:
       Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
           a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
           b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years, or;
           c. extended to a longer time period?
       Response:
       Transmission projects are complex and costly in nature, but for good reason. They involve

significant planning, engineering, siting, permitting, construction, and maintenance activities that

occur in phases over many years, resulting in safe and reliable infrastructure investments that serve

Texans for generations. Naturally, these are capital-intensive activities, and the results of these

LCRA COMMENTS                                                                           Page 3 of 23
 long-term investments are transmission system assets that provide additional capacity and

congestion relief to the grid as a whole for many decades. These transmission system assets make

up a network of infrastructure that all users of the system benefit from, so it has been deemed

reasonable in the past to allocate these costs to all users of the system in a generally uniform

fashion. However, with the influx of large loads seeking interconnection, state leadership and the

Commission have appropriately recognized that adjustments need to be made to this process. As

discussed in Commission Staff’s report in Project No. 58484, the 4CP methodology of cost

allocation is susceptible to sophisticated large loads shifting the burden of transmission costs

disproportionately to residential consumers that do not have similar abilities to precisely respond

during 4CP intervals. These actions obscure the price signals that are intended to result from

periods of high demand and result in less accurate reflections of cost responsibility relative to the

system improvements built to serve that demand.

       The proposed structure of the minimum billing demand mechanism makes large loads

accountable for the capacity they request and contract for, and the draft rules takes steps to ensure

those large loads will be long-term partners in sharing in the cost recovery of transmission assets

that all users of the grid benefit from having in service. LCRA supports applying this mechanism

for a fixed duration for simplicity purposes and to also encourage reasonable load ramp requests.

When determining duration, LCRA recommends that the Commission appropriately balance

transmission construction timelines that are necessary for phased large load ramp schedules, as

well as a reasonable duration that respects mature business viability for large loads.

       One concern that the proposal does not presently account for is an enforcement mechanism;

in the situation where a large load interconnects but ceases operations before the minimum billing




LCRA COMMENTS                                                                            Page 4 of 23
 demand duration is reached, it is not clear how TCOS recovery from that facility will be pursued.4

The Commission could either require financial security protections to cover the remaining duration

of the minimum billing demand period or consider whether a one-time penalty should be assessed.


        Question 3:
        Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand lower
        than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large load
        minimum bulling demand:
             a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
                 some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
                 demand in previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in phases
                 over the years, and how?
             b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
                 load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
                 customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous year
                 and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
                 weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases over
                 the years, and how?
        Response:
        These suggested methods introduce more complexity to the process than is necessary.

LCRA supports limiting the minimum billing demand to the large load customer’s approved ramp

scheduled for the current month and year. The effect of this approach will introduce a phased

limitation of the mechanism that more closely tracks along with transmission project timelines and

cost causation. LCRA offers related revisions to the PFP language below.

        Question 4:
       Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an
       entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
       Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
       electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
       cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
       legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational
       loads.
       Response:
       Large computational loads (LCLs) should not receive separate rate treatment and should

be subject to the same approach that all loads over the defined large load threshold (i.e., 75 MW)

ultimately receive. LCLs do introduce a unique level of risk during frequency and voltage

excursions, but that risk has been appropriately handled by the Commission’s approval of Nodal

Operating Guide Revision Request (NOGRR) 282, Large Computational Load Ride-Through

Requirements. NOGRR282 imposes an obligation on LCLs to ensure that their facilities can

comply with specific performance requirements, but LCLs do not introduce a unique level of

transmission costs or financial risks that would necessitate separate rate treatment.


       Question 5:
       Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the
       transmission capacity needs of a particular load?
       Response:
       No, and to do so would risk “double-counting” the transmission system costs that will be

paid for by large loads under the methodology proposed in this project. Transmission projects not

directly associated with the interconnecting facilities are separate and distinct in terms of their

need, benefit, and cost attribution. Remote transmission projects identified as part of a batch study

are better categorized as network upgrades. Network upgrades benefit all those served by ERCOT




LCRA COMMENTS                                                                           Page 6 of 23
 and are best handled via the Transmission Cost of Service allocation methodology, including a

minimum billing demand directly tied to the Large Load’s contracted load ramp amounts.


        Question 6:
        If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
        the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should these
        loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and transmission
        planning studies?
        Response:
        It is necessary to treat large load capacity according to the ramp schedules arising from the

current and future batch studies. This data is important to inform resource adequacy studies and

ensure that the Commission and ERCOT are working together to ensure that the appropriate market

signals are present to encourage supply to keep pace with expected demand. However, there is a

noticeable disconnect in the batch study related to resource adequacy concerns. During the July

2026 meeting of the Technical Advisory Committee, ERCOT made clear that the preliminary batch

zero load forecast (205 gigawatts) will potentially exceed what is available in the generation

interconnection queue for the corresponding time horizon of the study period. If this exceedance

comes to fruition during the batch study, ERCOT will have to use a defined pathway5 to gross up

capacity values in the generation interconnection queue in order to get the power flow cases to

solve. Although it was necessary to delay the Reliability Standard study to incorporate the batch

zero results into the load forecast, LCRA is discouraged by the delay on addressing the imminent

resource adequacy concerns and reiterates its comments made in the ERCOT stakeholder process.6

Numerous resource adequacy studies have indicated that ERCOT lacks sufficient long-duration

The PUC, ERCOT, and stakeholders should begin these discussions now to ensure that the market

is prepared to keep up with the magnitude, pace, and characteristics of expected load growth.

Delaying action only increases the risk of a mismatch between market signals and future reliability

needs.


                       III.     COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Duration of Coincident Peak and Improved Definitions - §25.192(b)

         It is clear that a change needs to be made to the existing 4CP process, and a transition to a

12CP approach is a reasonable policy change for the Commission to direct. This shift will

introduce greater variability to TSP billing units, which is undesirable from an efficiency

standpoint, but it will also provide some mitigation to cost-shifting behavior that is present today

in the wholesale market. An added benefit of the proposed methodology is the extension of the

coincident peak to a duration longer than 15 minutes. In previous comments, LCRA had proposed

an adjustment to this duration of no less than two hours. With compromise in mind, LCRA suggests

modifying the proposed 30-minute duration to one hour. Not only will this go one step further in

capturing a load’s normal usage behavior and better reflect its actual use of the transmission

system, but it will enhance mitigation of load curtailment behaviors that are not directly linked to

wholesale market price signals. Additionally, market participant systems have already been

designed to consume and process 15-minute and one-hour interval data for settlement purposes. A

Transmission Interconnection Costs - § 25.192(b)(13)

       The definition of transmission interconnection costs in 16 TAC § 25.192(b)(13) should be

clarified to avoid confusion and overlap with transmission interconnection costs that are addressed

in 16 TAC § 25.195 (relating to transmission-level generator interconnections) and to better sync

to the definitions that are being developed in Project No. 58481 (relating to Large Load



LCRA COMMENTS                                                                       Page 10 of 23
 Interconnection Standards). Specifically, “transmission interconnection costs” as that term is used

in proposed 16 TAC § 25.192 should align strictly with the term “direct interconnection costs” in

proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9).

       LCRA offers the following revisions to the definition and associated language to avoid

encompassing other transmission-level entities (i.e., generation resource entities) and other types

of costs that are best addressed through the revised cost allocation methodology than through direct

assignment:

       (13)    Transmission interconnection costs -- All direct interconnection costs associated

               with the facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection

               of a transmission-level large load customer, or a distinct set of transmission-level

               large load customers, to the existing transmission network, including

               interconnection lines, substation additions or modifications, and associated

               equipment necessary to establish or modify service.

Transmission Cost of Service - § 25.192(e)(6)

       For the same reasons that modifications are needed to the definition of “transmission

interconnection costs” in proposed subsection (b)(13), the language in subsection (e)(6) should be

similarly modified to avoid unintentionally impacting interconnection agreements with

transmission-connected generators. Cost recovery for generator interconnections was specifically

addressed by the Legislature in House Bill 1500 (88th R.S.), requiring the Commission to develop

a reasonable allowance applicable to certain generation resources; that policy should not be

disturbed by this rulemaking.




LCRA COMMENTS                                                                         Page 11 of 23
        LCRA offers the following revisions to this section to avoid impacting cost recovery for

transmission-connected generation resources:

       (6)     Notwithstanding any other provision of this section, transmission interconnection

               costs associated with large load interconnection agreements signed after the

               effective date of this section must not be included in a TSP’s transmission cost of

               service or transmission service rates.

12CP Clarity - § 25.192(f)(1)

       Since the superseding coincident peak periods will overlap two different years, the rule

language should modify “current year” to “current period” to prevent confusion. In addition to this

suggestion, LCRA also offers revisions to incorporate a requirement for ERCOT to file both the

unadjusted and adjusted 12CP values. Finally, LCRA requests updates to the rule language to

clearly define the scenarios where the Commission will consider modifications to the 12CP values.

       LCRA offers the following revisions to this section to effectuate these recommendations:

       (1)     12CP. No later than December 1 of each year, ERCOT must determine and file

               with the commission the current year period’s DSP 12CP unadjusted and adjusted

               load for each DSP, based on the ERCOT 12CP intervals ending the immediately

               preceding September. ERCOT must also include in this filing the ERCOT 12CP

               unadjusted and adjusted load for the current year period. The measurement of the

               ERCOT system monthly peak demand for purposes of determining the ERCOT

               12CP intervals and the determination of the DSP demand values that coincide with

               the ERCOT 12CP intervals must be in accordance with ERCOT protocols. The

               commission may approve changes to DSP 12CP values and the ERCOT 12CP value

               at any time

 Commission-Initiated Rate Revision - §25.192(i)

          The PFP improperly seeks to expand the Commission’s statutory authority by allowing the

Commission to require any TSP to file an application to revise its transmission rates at any time.

Under PURA, the Commission has the authority to initiate a rate-change proceeding only if, “after

reasonable notice and hearing, [it] finds that the existing rates of an electric utility for a service are

unreasonable or in violation of law.”10 The Commission exercises this oversight through 16 TAC

§ 25.73, pursuant to which it requires each TSP to file “a report that will permit the commission to

monitor its transmission costs and revenues.” Absent the required statutory showing that the TSP

is over-earning or its rates otherwise violate the law, the Commission has no authority to require a

TSP to file an application to revise its rates—and even then, it may do so only following the notice

and hearing procedures set forth in PURA. The final sentence in section (i) of the PFP is contrary

to this legislative grant of authority and should be stricken from the final rule as shown below.

(i)       Revision of transmission rates. Each TSP in the ERCOT region must periodically revise

          its transmission rates under this section to reflect changes in the cost of providing such

          services. Any request for a change in transmission rates must comply with the filing

          requirements established by the commission. The commission may, at any time, require a

          TSP to file an application to revise its rates.

Commission-Mandated Filing Schedule - § 25.192(j)(6)

          The PFP improperly seeks to expand the Commission’s statutory authority by allowing the

Commission to prescribe a schedule for TSPs to file proceedings to revise the rates for transmission

services, without limitation to which TSPs the schedule may apply. However, the rate review

schedule provision in PURA is specifically limited to “only to an electric utility, other than a river

a rate review schedule for a TSP that is a river authority—i.e., LCRA TSC. This section of the PFP

is contrary to law and should be revised in the final rule as shown below to match the authority

granted to the Commission under PURA § 36.157.

           (6)          Filing schedule. The commission may prescribe a schedule for TSPs electric

                        utilities, other than river authorities, that operate solely inside ERCOT to file

                        proceedings to revise the rates for transmission services.

Offset of Revenue Requirements and Necessary Coordination - § 25.192(k)(2)

           Through the minimum billing demand provisions, this PFP will ensure that large loads

appropriately contribute to transmission cost recovery as the ERCOT transmission system is

upgraded over time. It is also clear that the PFP will require TSPs to apply all interconnection fees

and forfeited financial security amounts as an offset to the TSP’s transmission revenue requirement

following adoption of the rules. What is not clear, however, is how the rules in this project will

interact with the provisions of the Commission’s Large Load Interconnection Standards to be

developed in Project No. 58481 and adopted in 16 TAC § 25.194.

           As proposed in Project No. 58481, an Interconnecting Large Load Entity (ILLE) would be

required to fully securitize “system upgrades that are necessary to reliably serve the large load

customer.”12 If the ILLE subsequently withdraws before peak demand for the project is reached,

remaining financial security would be applied to outstanding amounts owed, and 20% of the

remaining balance would be returned to the ILLE. The remaining 80% would then be considered

 as a revenue offset in the TSP’s next interim rate proceeding or comprehensive rate proceeding.13

However, that 80% remainder would not reflect any costs that the TSP actually incurred, so it is

not clear why the balance would need to offset the TSP’s transmission revenue requirement. The

far better approach would be to refund to the ILLE the full amount of posted security not drawn

upon to make the TSP and its ratepayers whole, and address “system upgrade costs” in their

entirety through 16 TAC § 25.192 and the revised TCOS allocation methodology that will be

            In other words, residential and small commercial ratepayers will be adequately protected

from stranded investment through the institution of a minimum billing demand charge as set forth

in this PFP, and by requiring ILLEs to fully fund—through Contribution in Aid of Construction

(CIAC)—the full amount of the direct costs necessary to physically interconnect them. By contrast,

any amounts securitized by the TSP for system upgrades should have no impact on the TSP’s

revenue requirement if the ILLE withdraws its request and those transmission system investments

are never undertaken. Accordingly, 16 TAC § 25.192(k) and 16 TAC § 25.194(g) should be

harmonized to limit the TSP’s revenue requirement offset to only the interconnection fees incurred

by the TSP and to ensure that direct interconnection costs for large load interconnections are

funded by CIAC, but otherwise allowing securitized system upgrade costs to be returned to the

ILLE less any costs actually incurred by the TSP.

       In terms of the minimum billing demand charge, it is clear in the PFP that the large load

customer’s billing must commence at the level of available service at the time it is available. Also,

when reviewing the Distribution Service Provider (DSP) Transmission Cost Recovery Factor

(TCRF) formula, there is a clear linkage to updates associated with the minimum billing demand.

Additionally, the batch zero study window covers years 2028 through 2032, so LCRA’s assumption

is that the first available service window for a large load studied through this process will be

January 2028, and therefore the first year where minimum billing demand will be captured is 2029.

Absent further clarity, below are LCRA’s high-level assumptions on how this transition will take

place for a new large load that begins receiving transmission service after January 1, 2028:

Regardless, a transition process schedule (preferably with more detail) is necessary for all parties

Minimum Billing Demand - §25.193(d) and §25.252(e)(2)

            LCRA is supportive of the minimum billing demand mechanism. However, as pointed out

previously in these comments, the proposed rule does not account for the situation where a facility

interact with the provisions of the Commission's Large Load Interconnection Standards to be
